S1_incident_reporting.quote: Manufacturers must report every confirmed thermal incident involving overheating, smoke, fire, or thermal injury to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, with a preliminary account of known risks and response steps. Within 72 hours of learning of an incident, manufacturers must notify the affected unit's customer of known immediate safety steps and how to obtain updates.

S2_thermal_testing.quote: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol and a representative sample, with failures and sample size reported. The maximum permitted failure rate is 5% per model. Manufacturers must provide complete per-model results to the relevant regulator and provide results to customers who request results for their own model; individual-company failure rates need not be published publicly. ... Exceeding 5% triggers regulatory review but does not by itself require an automatic ban; the regulator may require additional safeguards, restrict sales, or take other proportionate action based on the results and evidence of risk.

S3_remote_shutoff.quote: New home battery systems must include a remotely operable emergency shut-off that can be activated by the customer and, where an imminent safety risk warrants it, by the manufacturer with prompt customer notification. For units already installed when this standard is adopted, manufacturers must enable remote shut-off where technically supported within six years; where it is not supported, they must notify customers and provide an equivalent safe shut-off procedure.

S4_fire_suppression.quote: New home battery systems manufactured 36 months or more after adoption of this standard must include built-in fire suppression appropriate to the system's chemistry and installation, validated under a regulator-approved test protocol. Regulators may approve an equivalent protective design where it provides comparable mitigation of fire spread and risk to occupants and neighbours.

S5_customer_disclosure.quote: A recall is mandatory when a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in any 12-month period; the manufacturer must promptly notify the regulator and affected customers, stop new sales pending regulator review, and implement the regulator-approved recall or corrective action. Regulators may also require a recall where other evidence shows an unacceptable safety risk.

document.section_notes: All four red lines are respected: per-model results go to regulators and on request to purchasers of that model but are not publicly published (NW-1/HC-1), retrofit is 6 years (NW-2), and suppression starts at 36 months (HC-2). S2 keeps the 55 °C test and the 5% limit but explicitly removes any automatic sales ban, leaving consequences to regulator discretion, which weakens the teeth of the limit. S5 has a mandatory numeric 8/100k trigger but lets a regulator-approved corrective action substitute indefinitely, and S1 is strict (24h reporting of confirmed incidents) though it omits any requirement to report while the cause is still under investigation.
